title: Study Finds Sherloc Updates Reduced Uncertain Genetic Test Variants by 31%
summary: A 10-year Labcorp study found that ongoing updates to the Sherloc genetic variant classification framework reduced uncertain test variants by 31%, improving genetic interpretation.
body_markdown:
*Genetic testing can reveal important changes in DNA, but understanding what those findings mean for a patient's health can take time.*


New research from Labcorp, published in the **[Journal of Molecular Diagnostics ,](https://www.jmdjournal.org/article/S1525-1578(26)00160-1/abstract) examined how a classification framework that can rapidly adapt to new science and technology has changed the way genetic variants are interpreted.


Researchers found that ongoing updates to Sherloc, a framework used to classify genetic variants, helped resolve more uncertain findings as new evidence and tools became available.


## Why interpreting genetic test results can be challenging


Genetic testing analyzes a patient's DNA to look for changes that may be linked to health or disease. These changes are called genetic variants.


When there isn't enough evidence to determine whether a variant is harmless or disease-causing, it's classified as a **variant of uncertain significance (VUS)** . These findings can leave patients and providers without a clear answer as to whether the variant is related to a patient's health or condition.


New sources of genetic data and advanced analytical tools can provide information that wasn't available when a variant was first evaluated. As a result, some previously uncertain variants can later be reclassified.


## How Sherloc helps classify genetic findings ****


Once a genetic variant is identified, scientists evaluate the available evidence to understand what it may mean. Sherloc is a point-based framework based on established guidelines for genetic variant classification. Its scoring system weighs different types of evidence, such as how often it appears in the population and whether it has been linked to disease. This helps scientists determine if it should be classified as benign, disease-causing or uncertain.


##


## The impact of Sherloc updates


Researchers tracked 32,241 variants first evaluated with an earlier version of Sherloc and followed their classifications across later versions. The study found that updates to Sherloc helped resolve more uncertain findings.


- Over the study period, 11% of all tracked variants were reclassified, and the number of variants classified as uncertain fell by 31%
- Of the 3,834 uncertain variants that were reclassified, 73% relied on criteria added in newer versions of Sherloc


In a separate analysis, researchers simulated removing newer AI-related criteria and found that about 1 in 5 variants would have been classified as uncertain without them. Together, the findings suggest that keeping classification frameworks up to date with new evidence and tools may help provide patients with more information to support follow-up testing and care.


Since Sherloc was introduced in 2017, it has continued to evolve alongside advances in genetic science. Across 19 versions, Sherloc has been used to classify about 2.6 million variants from 5.5 million people referred for genetic testing.


## Helping patients and families decide what to do next


When a patient receives an uncertain result, a natural question is, "What should I do next?" One option is to test family members to see whether the variant runs alongside disease in the family. The study found that Sherloc's evidence scores can help guide this decision, identifying which uncertain results are most likely to be resolved through family testing and helping patients and families receive clearer answers sooner.


## Applying new discoveries to genetic testing


As genetic science advances, so can the way scientists classify genetic variants. Sherloc has expanded to include larger population databases, DNA-RNA analysis and machine learning approaches. The study also suggests that certain Sherloc criteria may help identify situations in when additional testing, including family testing, could be useful.


“The science behind genomic variant interpretation is advancing at a remarkable pace, driven by new technologies and an expanding body of genetic evidence. To deliver the highest-quality, most accurate answers for patients, our interpretation frameworks must evolve alongside these advances while remaining evidence-based, systematic and scientifically rigorous,” said Yuya Kobayashi, Ph.D., lead author of the study. “Sherloc was built with exactly that goal in mind. This study demonstrates how a structured, continuously refined framework can incorporate new scientific insights to reduce uncertainty in genetic test results, helping more patients and providers make informed decisions about follow-up testing, risk assessment and care.”


**Read the study:**[The ten-year evolution of Sherloc, a points-based framework for genetic variant classification](https://www.jmdjournal.org/article/S1525-1578(26)00160-1/abstract) *,* published in *Journal of Molecular Diagnostic* s.


## About the Authors


**Marjorie Jody Westbrook, Ph.D.,** is a senior lead on the Clinical Science team at Labcorp, where she provides scientific leadership in genomic variant curation and clinical translation. She holds a Bachelor of Science in biology from the University of Virginia and a Ph.D. in Molecular and Cell Biology from the University of California, Berkeley. Dr. Westbrook has been instrumental in building and refining the scientific foundation of Labcorp's genetic testing portfolio, from early-stage condition curation across complex diseases to enhancing clinical content quality, curation updates and reporting improvements in close collaboration with cross-functional teams.


**Yuya Kobayashi, Ph.D.** , is a principal scientist at Labcorp, where he leads research and scientific strategy within the Genetic Insights Group focused on variant classification methodology and data-driven genomic insights. He holds a Bachelor of Science in Molecular and Cell Biology from the University of Washington and a Ph.D. in Genetics from Stanford University. With over 15 years of experience in the genomic variant interpretation space, Dr. Kobayashi's research has focused on leveraging AI-informed frameworks and other technological advances to improve variant classification at scale and reduce inequities in genomic interpretation across diverse patient populations.
